bibliographic.title: Human-supervised, large language model-based clinical decision support aligned to national newborn protocols in Kenya: a pragmatic, early-stage evaluation
bibliographic.authors: Kuria, T.; Kamau, G.; Makokha, F.; Omondi, P.; Mbugua, G.; Kamau, D.; Mbugua, S.; Gitaka, J.
bibliographic.citation_apa: Kuria, T., Kamau, G., Makokha, F., Omondi, P., Mbugua, G., Kamau, D., Mbugua, S., & Gitaka, J. (2026). Human-supervised, large language model-based clinical decision support aligned to national newborn protocols in Kenya: A pragmatic, early-stage evaluation. Frontiers in Digital Health, 8, 1832634. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1832634

methodology.study_design: prospective, mixed-methods, early-stage evaluation embedded in routine workflows at two public health facilities
methodology.sample_description: 50 trained healthcare workers; 550 neonatal cases over 10 months; surveyed HCWs n=33; 118 AI-generated recommendations reviewed by two neonatologists with third adjudicator; 40 complex dosing scenarios
methodology.sample_size: 550 neonatal cases; 50 HCWs trained; 33 surveyed HCWs; 118 recommendations reviewed
methodology.technology_context: AIFYA tablet-based CDSS integrating a fine-tuned generative LLM based on GPT-4 architecture with a structured knowledge base derived from Kenya national newborn and paediatric protocols; offline-first architecture; facility-based coaching model

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study provides empirical evidence on human-supervised, guideline-aligned LLM deployment in regulated newborn healthcare, including expert review, citation concordance, and workflow integration. Provided text describes a clinical decision support system with structured and unstructured clinician input, not a conversational, chatbot, or agentic interface; therefore it supports governance and oversight themes but is not central evidence for conversational governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter and early pages were supplied; conversational interaction model, guardrails, logging, audit, escalation, and full limitations sections are not visible and require full-text verification.

appraisal.notes: Methods appear appropriate for an early-stage AI evaluation under DECIDE-AI, with blinded expert adjudication and inter-rater reliability reporting. Generalizability beyond Kenyan newborn protocols and two facilities remains unclear from the excerpt.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are empirically reported and internally coherent for feasibility, accuracy, and adoption outcomes, but the supplied text is incomplete and the study is early-stage, site-limited, and not focused on conversational governance mechanisms.

coding.theme: Human-supervised LLM clinical decision support in regulated healthcare
coding.subtheme: Early-stage pragmatic evaluation of protocol-aligned newborn CDSS
rq_alignment: human oversight in regulated LLM systems
governance through protocol alignment and citation
operational deployment and monitoring in healthcare
accuracy and safety evaluation before scale-up

synthesis.main_claim: A human-supervised, guideline-aligned LLM-based CDSS (AIFYA) can be feasibly implemented in routine newborn care workflows in Kenyan public facilities, with acceptable recommendation accuracy, citation accuracy, and workflow adoption in an early-stage evaluation.
synthesis.contribution: Demonstrates a pragmatic, DECIDE-AI-guided evaluation of an LLM CDSS grounded in national protocols, combining adoption metrics, expert-reviewed recommendation quality, citation verification, and mixed-methods workflow assessment in a regulated clinical setting.
synthesis.limitations: Early-stage evaluation at two facilities; not a controlled effectiveness or safety trial; conversational interaction and broader governance mechanisms such as audit logs, tracing, contestation, and post-deployment monitoring are not evidenced in the supplied text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence for human supervision, protocol-grounded LLM deployment, and regulated-healthcare evaluation design; do not treat as primary evidence for conversational governance unless full text confirms dialogue-based interaction.
